name: Treaty with the Sioux, Sisseton and Wahpeton Bands, 1867
nations: Sisseton Wahpeton Oyate (Sisitunwan and Wahpetunwan Dakota)
promises: Article 3: a "permanent reservation" from the head of Lake Traverse along the 1851 treaty line to Lake Kampeska, for band members who had surrendered and were not sent to Crow Creek and those released from prison in 1866.
Article 4: a second reservation at Devils Lake for the other members of the bands and the Cut-Head Yanktonai.
Article 5: allotments of 160 acres to heads of families who settled to farm, with patents after five years that allowed no transfer except to the United States.
In return the bands ceded the right to build roads, railroads, mail stations and telegraph lines across the lands they claimed (Article 2).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission held that the Sisseton and Wahpeton had recognized title to the Devils Lake Reservation set apart by Article 4, and that three acts of the United States were Fifth Amendment takings requiring just compensation with interest: Army use of 11,313.08 acres as a military reserve for 23.25 years, the disposal of 64,908.22 acres left out by an erroneous 1875 survey, and the disposal of 105,839.30 unallotted acres under the Act of April 27, 1904.

breaches.what: The claim of the Sisseton-Wahpeton bands for about 8.7 million acres taken under the agreement of September 20, 1872, land the Commission had found they owned and ceded as defined in Article 2 of this treaty, was settled by compromise.

landTaken: Devils Lake Reservation: 11,313.08 acres used as a military reserve, 64,908.22 acres excluded by erroneous survey and 105,839.30 unallotted acres disposed of under the 1904 Act (Docket 363, 1973). The 1872 agreement concerned about 8.7 million acres (Docket 363, 1977).
compensation: Docket 363, Devils Lake claim: the 1973 order valued the use of the military reserve at $55,236.19; the other two values are not legible in the scan opened. After deducting payments, the Commission's opinion of January 16, 1974 fixed the recovery at $8,286,991.54 plus 5 percent simple interest on a principal of $1,888,162.46 from January 1, 1974 until paid, and a final award for the Sisseton and Wahpeton Bands was entered on February 27, 1974. Docket 363, 1977: a compromise final judgment of $13,129,661 for the bands who made the 1872 agreement, after deducting the $800,000 recited in that agreement from an agreed land value of $13,929,661.
today: In DeCoteau v. District County Court (March 3, 1975) the Supreme Court held that the 1891 Act ratifying the 1889 agreement "terminated the Lake Traverse Reservation", a ruling against the tribe on state jurisdiction. The Sisseton Wahpeton Oyate governs from the Lake Traverse area; the Devils Lake Reservation is home to the Spirit Lake Dakota.

nationVoice.summary: The Oyate's government page dates its reserved tract to the treaty of February 19, 1867, describing it as running from Lake Traverse along the 1851 treaty line to Lake Kampeska and just into North Dakota.

Audit 2026-11-08: the 1973 holdings (recognized title, three Fifth Amendment takings, 11,313.08, 64,908.22 and 105,839.30 acres, $55,236.19) and the 1977 compromise figures were checked against the documents. Added the Devils Lake final award: the February 27, 1974 award is badly scanned (it reads '$8.2RG.991.51'), so the amount is taken from the January 16, 1974 opinion, which twice gives $8,286,991.54.
Whether the 1974 award was paid and how it was shared with the Spirit Lake Tribe was not traced.

plain.promised: The Sisseton and Wahpeton were promised a permanent reservation at Lake Traverse and a second at Devils Lake, with family farms that could not be sold except to the United States.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission held in 1973 that the United States took Devils Lake Reservation land three times without just compensation: for an Army post, through a wrong survey, and under a 1904 Act.
plain.today: A 1974 final award gave the bands $8,286,991.54 plus interest for the Devils Lake land, and a 1977 compromise paid $13,129,661 for land taken under the 1872 agreement. In 1975 the Supreme Court held the Lake Traverse Reservation terminated.
